article.overview: A relay satellite transponder is the radio repeater carried by a relay spacecraft. It receives signals from a lunar surface asset or another spacecraft, changes their frequency and power as needed, and retransmits them to Earth or to another user, so that data can travel where a direct Earth link is blocked by the Moon. Publicly documented examples include China's Queqiao and Queqiao-2 relay satellites, which were launched in 2018 and 2024 [1][3], and ESA's Lunar Pathfinder, which is planned for lunar orbit [5][6]. Public specifications are sparse, so the values below are tied to named missions and sources.
article.description: A relay transponder is not usually a stand-alone instrument. It is the communications payload of a relay satellite, combining receivers, transmitters, amplifiers, and one or more antennas tuned to the frequency bands used by the surface assets, orbiters and ground stations it serves. In a simple "bent-pipe" relay, the satellite receives a signal on one band, amplifies it and retransmits it on another band. More capable designs can add channel multiplexing, onboard data handling, or navigation and timing functions. Because the transponder is part of a spacecraft, its performance depends on the satellite's antenna size, pointing, power supply and orbit as much as on the radio electronics themselves.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a relay transponder is to provide communications and, in some designs, navigation support for lunar missions. The Moon's far side cannot see Earth directly, and the lunar south pole has limited Earth visibility for many ground-station geometries. A relay in an orbit that can see both the far side and Earth, such as the Earth-Moon L2 halo orbit used by Queqiao [1], can carry data from a far-side lander and rover to Earth. Later relays in elliptical lunar orbits, such as Queqiao-2 [2][3] and the planned Lunar Pathfinder [5], are designed to provide long daily visibility of other regions, including the southern lunar hemisphere.
article.operating_principle: A relay transponder receives a radio signal from a surface or orbital user on an uplink band, processes it, and transmits it on a downlink band toward Earth or another user. The usable data rate depends on the bands, the antennas, the transmitted power, the receiver sensitivity and the distance between the satellite and each user. Queqiao, for example, communicated with the Chang'e-4 lander and rover on X-band and with the Earth ground station on S-band [1]. Queqiao-2 used X-band for surface links, Ka-band for payload data to Earth, and S-band for telemetry and commands [3]. Lunar Pathfinder's ESA description mentions a main X-band link with Earth, but the lunar-link band is not stated in the source used [5].
article.scientific_importance: Relay transponders matter because the far side of the Moon and parts of the south polar region cannot always reach Earth directly. Queqiao gave the Chang'e-4 lander and rover an Earth link from the far side, using a relay placed at the Earth-Moon L2 point [1]. Queqiao-2 was described as extending this capability to far-side and south-pole missions [2]. A relay also allows surface assets to send data without each carrying a large Earth-pointing antenna, which is a practical constraint for small landers and rovers, although the exact trade-off depends on mission design.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a relay transponder. The three examples serve different roles and orbits, and their mass, antenna and link values must not be compared as if they were the same design. Where a value is not publicly stated, it is recorded as not stated (null).

examples.name: Queqiao (Chang'e-4 relay satellite)
examples.mass_source_note: Pre-launch Planetary Society article; mass as announced before launch.
examples.communication_links: X-band with the Chang'e-4 lander and rover; S-band with the Earth ground station. Data rates not stated.
examples.power_system: Solar panels and lithium batteries. Power output in watts not stated.
examples.orbit: Earth-Moon L2 halo orbit, reached after a lunar swing-by about 8 to 9 days after launch. L2 is about 450,000 km from Earth and more than 60,000 km from the farside lander and rover. Halo orbit size and period not stated.
examples.launch: Long March 4C from Xichang Satellite Launch Centre, May 2018 (planned start 21 May per pre-launch article).
examples.planned_design_life: More than 5 years (planned; not a demonstrated lifetime).
examples.other_payloads: Netherlands-China Low-Frequency Explorer (NCLE) for low-frequency radio astronomy; 170 mm laser retroreflector for Earth-Queqiao laser ranging.
examples.unverified_notes: Entry into the L2 halo orbit in June 2018 is reported in secondary summaries and was not verified against a primary CNSA source.

examples.name: Queqiao-2 (Chang'e-6 relay satellite)
examples.mass_source_note: Wikipedia labels 1,200 kg as dry mass in the infobox and as take-off weight including 488 kg of hydrazine and oxidiser in the design section. The label is unresolved.
examples.antenna: 4.2 m deployable parabolic reflector with stated gain of 44 dBi; separate 0.6 m Ka-band dish on the nadir side.
examples.communication_links: X-band surface links with 10 simultaneous channels each way; Ka-band payload data to Chinese Academy of Sciences ground stations, about 100 Mbit/s average; S-band telemetry and commands at 2,000 bit/s uplink and 4,096 bit/s downlink, with payload data up to 6 Mbit/s as backup. Uplink from surface robots is 50 kbit/s via omni antenna or 5 Mbit/s via the parabolic antenna. These values come from a secondary encyclopaedia and have not been verified against a primary source; the same article's comparison table gives a different X-band rate (1 kbit/s) that is unresolved.
examples.power_system: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.orbit: Planned: elliptical frozen orbit of about 200 by 16,000 km, 24-hour period, inclination 62.4 degrees. Later planned switch to a 12-hour-period orbit for south-pole missions (Planetary Society). Reported reached orbit: infobox gives about 254.3 by 16,941.1 km at 119.249 degrees retrograde with a 26.18-hour period; the article's body text gives 1992 by 18679 km and contradicts itself on whether the planned orbit was entered. Reached-orbit figures are unresolved.
examples.launch: 20 March 2024 00:31:28 UTC, Long March 8 from Wenchang. Lunar orbit insertion reported as 24 March 2024; the insertion time differs between sources (17:05 UTC and 16:46 UTC).
examples.other_payloads: Science payloads reported by the Planetary Society include GENA, EUC and LOVEX. Co-manifested CubeSats Tiandu-1 (61 kg, laser retroreflector, Ka dual-band communication payload) and Tiandu-2 (15 kg, communications instrument).
examples.unverified_notes: A secondary summary of the LOVEX paper reports an apoapsis of about 160,000 km, which differs from the encyclopaedia figure; unresolved.

examples.name: Lunar Pathfinder
examples.type: Planned commercial lunar relay satellite (ESA anchor customer; built by SSTL)
examples.status: Planned / not flown as of sources reviewed
examples.mass_source_note: Not stated in the ESA or SSTL sources reviewed. Trade-press summaries that give a mass were not confirmed by a primary source and are not used.
examples.dimensions: Described by ESA as washing-machine-sized; dimensions not stated.
examples.communication_links: Main X-band transmitter links with Earth (ESA). Lunar-link band not stated in the ESA article. Relay role for orbiters and surface assets; S-band Proximity-1 protocol used with the user terminal for commissioning (SSTL). Data rates and number of users not stated. QinetiQ is reported as supplier of a Lunar Link Transponder without stating the flown unit.
examples.orbit: Elliptical lunar frozen orbit for prolonged coverage over the South Pole (ESA); daily visibility of the southern lunar hemisphere (SSTL). Altitude, inclination and period not stated.
examples.launch: Delivery to lunar orbit by Firefly's Blue Ghost transfer vehicle under NASA CLPS CS-3 (SSTL). Launch timing unresolved: ESA's 2022 caption says ready for launch at the end of 2024; a 2026 trade report says Blue Ghost Mission 2 is in assembly and environmental testing. Public sources reviewed do not confirm a launch date.
examples.other_payloads: ESA NaviMoon GNSS receiver (mass 1.4 kg; designed by SpacePNT, built by EECL; planned positioning accuracy better than 100 m at more than 400,000 km from Earth); NASA laser retroreflector developed by KBR; ESA radiation monitor.
examples.unverified_notes: Several secondary search summaries gave a launch mass, lunar-link band and design life for Lunar Pathfinder; none were confirmed in a primary source reviewed here, so they are recorded as null.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are not uniformly published. Queqiao's 4.2 m antenna and Queqiao-2's 4.2 m parabolic reflector are stated antenna sizes, not spacecraft dimensions. Lunar Pathfinder is described only as washing-machine-sized by ESA. The antenna size and orbit of each relay determine the coverage and data-rate envelope, so dimensions must be read together with mission geometry.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Queqiao: 425 kg (pre-launch figure). Queqiao-2: 1,200 kg, with the dry-mass versus take-off-weight label unresolved. Lunar Pathfinder: not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The NaviMoon receiver alone is 1.4 kg.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Queqiao uses solar panels and lithium batteries; its output in watts is not stated in the source used. Queqiao-2 and Lunar Pathfinder power outputs are not stated in the sources reviewed. Propulsion and station-keeping propellant for Queqiao-2 is reported as 488 kg of hydrazine and oxidiser, subject to the label caveat above.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A relay satellite operates in the lunar environment and in cislunar space. It must tolerate large temperature swings, radiation and micrometeoroid exposure, and it must keep its antennas accurately pointed at Earth or at surface users. Queqiao-type halo-orbit operation requires station-keeping because the L2 point is dynamically unstable, and an elliptical lunar orbit requires periodic orbit maintenance and visibility planning. These are general engineering constraints; the sources reviewed for this article do not give the detailed environmental qualification levels for any named relay transponder.
article.limitations: A single relay provides one communications path and, for the navigation-capable designs, a limited navigation function. Its performance depends on antenna geometry, orbit visibility, frequency coordination and the users it serves. Published data rates and link budgets are often system-level and may not describe the transponder alone. The relay transponder class also covers several mission architectures, so any single figure applies only to the named mission.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A relay satellite is an orbiter-type payload. Its transportation chain is spacecraft integration on Earth, launch, Earth-Moon transfer, lunar orbit insertion, commissioning and operations. The three examples used different routes: Queqiao used a lunar swing-by to reach L2; Queqiao-2 was inserted into lunar orbit after launch on Long March 8; Lunar Pathfinder is to be delivered to lunar orbit by a commercial transfer vehicle.
transportation_process: Integrate the relay satellite with its launch vehicle and transfer stage on Earth.
Launch from Earth (Queqiao: Long March 4C from Xichang; Queqiao-2: Long March 8 from Wenchang).
Transfer to the Moon, including a lunar swing-by to reach Earth-Moon L2 for Queqiao (about 8 to 9 days after launch).
Insert into the target lunar or Earth-Moon orbit; Queqiao-2 insertion reported 24 March 2024.
Lunar Pathfinder: deliver to lunar orbit by Firefly's Blue Ghost transfer vehicle under NASA CLPS CS-3 (SSTL).
Commission the satellite and bring up its lunar-link and Earth-link services; interface details not publicly specified.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Relay satellites are not landed; they are placed in orbit. No surface deployment is involved. Antenna deployment (for example Queqiao-2's deployable parabolic reflector) is a spacecraft-level event whose timing and mechanism are not described in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Queqiao (2018) at Earth-Moon L2 relayed for the Chang'e-4 lander and rover. Queqiao-2 (2024) relayed for Chang'e-6 and is planned for Chang'e-7 (2026) and Chang'e-8 (2028) per the Planetary Society. Lunar Pathfinder is planned to be delivered by Blue Ghost Mission 2.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Lunar Pathfinder's delivery by Firefly's Blue Ghost transfer vehicle is stated by SSTL. No further compatibility with any specific lander, transfer vehicle or launch vehicle is verified in this article. Mass, mounting and interface data needed for a compatibility assessment are not publicly specified for Lunar Pathfinder.

article.historical_significance: Queqiao was the first lunar relay satellite placed at the Earth-Moon L2 point, and it supported the Chang'e-4 lander and rover on the far side [1]. Queqiao-2 later extended China's relay capability to Chang'e-6 and to planned south-pole missions [2][3]. NASA's Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS) programme is a parallel effort to create commercial lunar relay and navigation services as part of the Near Space Network. In 2024 NASA selected Intuitive Machines as the first commercial LCRNS service provider, and NASA states that its goal is for multiple providers to supply lunar communications and navigation capabilities [4]. LCRNS is a programme and service model, not a single transponder design, and the NASA page does not give transponder hardware specifications [4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The phrase "relay satellite transponder" describes a function within a spacecraft rather than one standard design. Queqiao, Queqiao-2 and Lunar Pathfinder use different orbits, bands and antenna sizes, and their figures are not interchangeable. Queqiao-2's reached orbit is inconsistent across the sources reviewed [3]. The Lunar Pathfinder launch date, mass, lunar-link band and design life are not confirmed by the primary sources reviewed [5][6][8]. Queqiao-2 link rates come from a secondary encyclopaedia and need primary verification [3]. No official source reviewed here gives transponder frequency plans, link budgets or G/T values for Lunar Pathfinder. The LCRNS page provides no transponder specifications [4]. Image assets were not verified, so this article contains no embedded images.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No images were verified in this run, so the image registry is empty.

data_quality_notes: Queqiao-2 reached-orbit figures are inconsistent within the Wikipedia article (infobox versus body text, and a contradiction about whether the planned orbit was entered). A secondary summary of the LOVEX paper gives a different apoapsis. Unresolved.
Queqiao-2 mass label (dry mass versus take-off weight including propellant) is inconsistent in the Wikipedia source. Unresolved.

Queqiao-2 link rates and the X-band rate (50 kbit/s and 1 kbit/s in different parts of the same secondary article) come from a secondary encyclopaedia and have not been verified against CNSA or peer-reviewed primary sources.
Queqiao: launch timing and entry into the L2 halo orbit in June 2018 are based on pre-launch and secondary sources; not verified against a primary CNSA source. Mass is a pre-launch figure.

Lunar Pathfinder: launch date unresolved (ESA 2022 readiness at end of 2024; 2026 trade report on Blue Ghost Mission 2 testing; search summaries differ on late 2026 versus 2027). Mass, dimensions, lunar-link band, antenna, power and design life are not stated in the primary sources reviewed. Search-summary figures for mass, lunar-link band and design life were not confirmed and are not used.

The SpaceOps-2023 Lunar Pathfinder paper (publications.spaceops.org, id 0339) could not be read in this run (the PDF returned binary content that could not be extracted). Transponder frequency plans, data rates and link budgets remain unverified.
The NASA LCRNS page gives no transponder hardware specifications, launch dates or relay counts. LCRNS is a service programme rather than a single payload.
No images were verified from official pages in this run; the image registry is empty and no image URLs were invented. Image research remains open.
